steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on robot skill learning for sample scraping in a chemistry lab. Motivate why lab automation needs learned skills beyond pre-programmed motions, describe our reinforcement learning and curriculum approach and the move to a real robot, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Materials discovery and robot scientists
2. The gap: lab robots limited to pre-programmed manipulation
3. Why learning and dexterous skills matter: the sample scraping example
4. Our approach: model-free RL with curriculum learning, simulation to real robot
5. Contributions
6. Novelty and real-lab evaluation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Materials discovery and robot scientists
- addresses global challenges: renewable and clean energy storage, sustainable polymers, drugs and therapeutics, consumer packaging -> circular economy
- 'robot scientists' support humans with long-term experiments for new materials
- robots: tedious cognitive and manual tasks; humans: safe, mentally stimulating experiments

2. The gap
- remarkable progress in lab automation, but nothing beyond pre-programmed manipulation
- hinders end-to-end autonomous robots in human labs, continuing experiments after hours, novel protocols

3. Learning and dexterity
- most lab robots: pre-defined point-to-point motions, no sensory feedback, no learning
- learning handles environmental variation: lighting conditions, displaced material
- humans: different modalities, skills improve with experience
- not attainable with traditional automation: dexterity, visual input / motor response coordination (trivial in humans)
- robots have acquired practical skills not previously possible
- dexterous manipulation enables many useful workflows
- example: sample scraping (Fig. 1): chemist scrapes vial walls, translating vertically in a circular fashion
- needs force feedback; different crystal morphology needs adaptive scraping

4. Approach
- model-free RL for lab automation; skill acquisition in material discovery workflows
- policies for full scraping task: proprioceptive + force observations -> end effector displacement actions
- curriculum learning: extend workspace size as training performance improves; lower training cost, higher task success
- learns harder insertion + scraping task; RL without curriculum fails
- trained and evaluated in simulation; adjustments + findings when moving to real robot

5. Contributions
- closed-loop formulation of in-tube scraping (sub-task of crystallisation workflow)
- new benchmark: closed-space manipulation and extraction of material
- case study: deep RL for in-tube scraping
- curriculum learning for insertion + scraping
- demonstration in simulation and real-world Chemistry lab

6. Novelty
- first learning-based human-inspired motor skills for crystallisation workflow in a real Chemistry lab
- setup with tools and glassware from a real material discovery lab

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Transforming materials discovery is very important for addressing global challenges, for example renewable and clean energy storage, sustainable polymers, drugs and therapeutics, and packaging for consumer products towards a more circular economy. To make fundamental breakthroughs in this field happen more often, human scientists can be supported by 'robot scientists' that carry out the long-term experiments that are key to getting new materials. The goal is that robots do tedious cognitive and manual tasks, while humans do experiments that are safe and mentally stimulating. There has been remarkable progress in bringing robotics into laboratory automation, but there is still an open gap in having robots do tasks beyond pre-programmed manipulation. This holds back progress on autonomous robots that can work end-to-end in human labs, or at least continue the scientists' experiments after hours and support novel experimental protocols.

So far, most laboratory robotics relies on pre-defined point-to-point motions without any sensory feedback or learning-based methods that would make them more adaptable to different environmental conditions. Learning would help with the problem of environmental variation, because learning algorithms can adapt to variations in lighting conditions, displacements of material, etc. Humans, on the other hand, can use different modalities and do skills that get better with experience. This is not, and will never be, possible with traditional laboratory automation, because of the dexterity and coordination between visual inputs and motor response that is needed, which is trivial in humans. In turn, robots were able to learn a variety of practical skills that were not possible before. Solving dexterous manipulation in laboratory tasks is an important problem, since it enables a wide range of useful robotic workflows that are otherwise not possible. Consider for example the sample scraping problem shown in Fig. 1. A human chemist would scrape the vial walls by moving vertically in a circular fashion. This kind of task cannot be solved with traditional laboratory automation methods, because force feedback is needed as the walls are scraped and different crystal morphology needs an adaptive way of scraping.

4. Approach
- model-free RL for lab automation; skill acquisition in material discovery workflows
- policies for full scraping task: proprioceptive + force observations -> end effector displacement actions
- curriculum learning: extend workspace size as training performance improves; lower training cost, higher task success
- learns harder insertion + scraping task; RL without curriculum fails
- trained and evaluated in simulation; adjustments + findings when moving to real robot

- closed-loop formulation of in-tube scraping (sub-task of crystallisation workflow)
- new benchmark: closed-space manipulation and extraction of material
- case study: deep RL for in-tube scraping
- curriculum learning for insertion + scraping
- demonstration in simulation and real-world Chemistry lab

- first learning-based human-inspired motor skills for crystallisation workflow in a real Chemistry lab

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Transforming materials discovery is very important for addressing global challenges, for example renewable and clean energy storage, sustainable polymers, drugs and therapeutics, and packaging for consumer products towards a more circular economy. To make fundamental breakthroughs in this field happen more often, human scientists can be supported by 'robot scientists' that carry out the long-term experiments that are key to getting new materials. The goal is that robots do tedious cognitive and manual tasks, while humans do experiments that are safe and mentally stimulating. There has been remarkable progress in bringing robotics into laboratory automation, but there is still an open gap in having robots do tasks beyond pre-programmed manipulation. This holds back progress on autonomous robots that can work end-to-end in human labs, or at least continue the scientists' experiments after hours and support novel experimental protocols.

So far, most laboratory robotics relies on pre-defined point-to-point motions without any sensory feedback or learning-based methods that would make them more adaptable to different environmental conditions. Learning would help with the problem of environmental variation, because learning algorithms can adapt to variations in lighting conditions, displacements of material, etc. Humans, on the other hand, can use different modalities and do skills that get better with experience. This is not, and will never be, possible with traditional laboratory automation, because of the dexterity and coordination between visual inputs and motor response that is needed, which is trivial in humans. In turn, robots were able to learn a variety of practical skills that were not possible before. Solving dexterous manipulation in laboratory tasks is an important problem, since it enables a wide range of useful robotic workflows that are otherwise not possible. Consider for example the sample scraping problem shown in Fig. 1. A human chemist would scrape the vial walls by moving vertically in a circular fashion. This kind of task cannot be solved with traditional laboratory automation methods, because force feedback is needed as the walls are scraped and different crystal morphology needs an adaptive way of scraping.

In this work we look at using model-free reinforcement learning (RL) in laboratory automation to overcome the previous challenges in skill acquisition for material discovery experimental workflows. We learn policies for the full laboratory task of scraping, and these map proprioceptive and force observations to end effector displacement actions of a robotic arm. We also explore curriculum learning, where the difficulty of the task is increased step by step by extending the size of the workspace as the training performance of the agent gets better, which reduces training costs and increases overall task success. This way we could learn the more challenging insertion and scraping task, while the RL method without a curriculum fails to learn it. Finally, the training and evaluation of the scraping policy is done in simulation, but we also report the adjustments that were needed and what we found when moving these policies to a real robotic platform.

The contributions of this work are:

- A closed-loop formulation of an in-tube scraping task, which is a sub-task of a crystallisation workflow.
- A new benchmark task for robot learning in labs: closed-space manipulation and extraction of material.
- A case study of applying deep reinforcement learning to a challenging motor skill (in-tube scraping) that traditional laboratory automation cannot do.
- Using curriculum learning to improve the learning performance of the RL agent in a more challenging insertion and scraping task.
- A demonstration of the learned robot behaviour in simulation and in a real-world Chemistry lab.

As far as we know, this is the first research that uses learning-based methods to acquire human-inspired motor skills for a crystallisation workflow in a real-world Chemistry laboratory. We evaluate the method with an experimental setup that uses tools and glassware from a real-world material discovery lab, to show that it is applicable to real laboratory environments.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Transforming materials discovery plays a pivotal role in addressing global challenges such as renewable and clean energy storage, sustainable polymers, drugs and therapeutics, and packaging for consumer products towards a more circular economy. To accelerate the frequency of fundamental breakthroughs in this field, human scientists can be supported by 'robot scientists' that carry out the long-term experiments key to obtaining new materials. The goal is for robots to carry out tedious cognitive and manual tasks, while humans conduct experiments that are safe and mentally stimulating. While there has been remarkable progress in introducing robotics to laboratory automation [1], [2], [3], [4], an open gap remains in having robots carry out tasks beyond pre-programmed manipulation. This hinders progress towards autonomous robots capable of operating end-to-end in human labs, or at the very least of continuing scientists' experiments after hours and supporting novel experimental protocols.

To date, most laboratory robotics relies on pre-defined point-to-point motions, without any sensory feedback or learning-based methods that would increase adaptability to differing environmental conditions. Learning would help tackle environmental variation, since learning algorithms can adapt to variations in lighting conditions, displacements of material, etc. Humans, conversely, are able to use different modalities and carry out skills that gradually improve with experience. This is not, and will never be, attainable with traditional laboratory automation because of the required dexterity and coordination between visual inputs and motor response, which is trivial in humans [5], [6]. In turn, robots have been able to acquire a variety of practical skills that were previously not possible [7]. Solving dexterous manipulation in laboratory tasks is an important problem, as it enables a wide range of useful robotic workflows that are otherwise not possible. Consider the sample scraping problem illustrated in Fig. 1. A human chemist would scrape the vial walls by translating vertically in a circular fashion. Such tasks cannot be solved with traditional laboratory automation methods, since force feedback is required as the walls are scraped and different crystal morphology calls for an adaptive method of scraping.

In this work, we investigate model-free reinforcement learning (RL) for laboratory automation to overcome previous challenges in skill acquisition for material discovery experimental workflows. We learn policies for the full laboratory task of scraping, which map proprioceptive and force observations to end effector displacement actions of a robotic arm. Moreover, we explore curriculum learning [8], [9], progressively increasing the difficulty of the task by extending the size of the workspace as the training performance of our agent improves, in order to reduce training costs while increasing overall task success. In this way we successfully learn the more challenging insertion and scraping task, whereas the RL method without a curriculum fails to learn. Finally, although training and evaluation of the scraping policy are performed in simulation, we report the adjustments required and our findings from migrating these policies to a real robotic platform.

In summary, the contributions of this work are:

- A closed-loop formulation of an in-tube scraping task, a sub-task of a crystallisation workflow.
- A new benchmark task for robot learning in labs: closed-space manipulation and extraction of material.
- A case study applying deep reinforcement learning to a challenging motor skill (in-tube scraping) that is not possible with traditional laboratory automation.
- Exploiting curriculum learning to improve the learning performance of the RL agent in a more challenging insertion and scraping task.
- A demonstration of the learned robot behaviour both in simulation and in a real-world Chemistry lab.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to use learning-based methods for acquiring human-inspired motor skills for a crystallisation workflow in a real-world Chemistry laboratory. We evaluate the method with an experimental setup using tools and glassware from a real-world material discovery lab, to demonstrate its applicability to real laboratory environments.
